books.section: The Rise of the Corporation and Mass Production
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

options.text: Easier incorporation laws, the railroad model, and the need for capital

options.misconception: Background: the government never banned small businesses; they kept operating alongside corporations.
options.text: The federal government’s ban on all small businesses

options.misconception: Background: competition stayed fierce; corporations were built to survive it, not to end it.
options.text: The end of all competition between American firms

options.misconception: Background: banks and financiers like J. P. Morgan funded the great corporations; they did not refuse them.
options.text: The refusal of banks to lend money to large companies

rationales.A: Background from the books: states eased incorporation before the war, railroads showed the model worked at scale, and only corporations could gather the capital that steel mills and railroads needed.
rationales.B: Background: small businesses did not vanish. Corporations grew beside them, and the passage starts with small firms still in business.
rationales.C: Background: the books stress cutthroat competition between firms. Corporations formed to win that competition, not because it had ended.
rationales.D: Background: financiers funded the new corporations. J. P. Morgan’s control of railroads and industry is the opposite of a refusal to lend.
rationales.general:
Combine the passage with what the books add.
1. The passage names two causes: easier incorporation laws and the railroad model.
2. Background from the books: railroads and steel mills needed more capital than any one owner could supply.
3. Only a corporation could gather that capital from many investors.
4. Together, law, model, and capital explain why the form spread.
Remember: a big change usually has more than one cause, so gather them all.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: Which of the following best explains why the corporation spread so widely after the Civil War?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage, written for this question from Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 8 (Topic 6.6), 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 18, and Princeton Review, Chapter 10.
stimulus.text: Before the Civil War, most American businesses were small firms run by their owners. After the war, new laws made it easier to form corporations, and the railroads showed how a corporation could work: the Pennsylvania Railroad, incorporated in 1846, grew into a business too large for any one owner to run. Large corporations hired layers of managers, kept careful cost accounts, and divided the work among departments for buying, selling, and shipping. A new class of middle managers ran the daily work while top executives planned for the future.
